326: Silk is a long fibre made mainly of "fibroin", taken from the silkworm's cocoon. Ah, "fibroin" is a kind of protein, you see, and the fibre spun from the silkworm's cocoon has a lustre all its own.
In your Japan, Touya, silk is called "kinu", I hear. There is cultivated silk and wild silk; wild silk comes from wild silkworms, such as tussah and tensan.
Cultivated silk, in turn, is either raw or degummed. Degummed silk is cocoon thread with the sericin on its surface removed.
Silk itself tires under repeated bending, but it stands up very well to impact.
And the silk thread, woven as warp and weft, becomes what we call "silk".
327: And the silk thread, woven as warp and weft, becomes what we call "silk".
328: Silk has a long history, and it has always been treasured throughout it.
It was first made long ago in China as a precious luxury, and was the chief trade good of the ancient Silk Road.
In ancient Rome it traded for its own weight in gold.
And how it was made stayed secret for a long time: anyone who took silkworms out of China was put to death.
329: "Silk", of course, runs from the cheap to the costly, but I cannot recommend the cheap kind. To feel what silk is truly worth, you must first know the genuine article.
The farmed silkworm I described gives cultivated silk; wild silkworms give tussah and tensan silk; and there are spun silk and fine silk thread too, each weaving a silk of its own character.
Above all, silk is lustrous, light and supple.
What's more, it takes dye beautifully, in a wide range of colours.
